speechtext:

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. Cole (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour):
subsubtopic: PURPOSES AND RESULTS OF OTTAWA CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for giving notice of his question. The national conference on apprenticeship in trade and industry had a threefold purpose:
1.	To review the facts respecting the alleged shortage of apprentices and trainees in skilled trades in all parts of Canada.
2.	To review existing apprenticeship plans and training programs in all provinces with a view to increasing their effectiveness where needed, and extending such programs to a degree which would meet the needs of all skilled trades.
3.	To obtain suggestions and recommendations from representatives of employers, organized labour, teachers of trades, and provincial government officials occupied in administration of training, regarding the best methods of increasing the number of apprentices and trainees in skilled trades and of developing co-operative and co-ordinated activities for the promotion and development of apprenticeship training in Canada.
Speaking in a general way, the results of the conference were as follows: The immediate results of the conference have been to bring to the attention of all interested that Canadian industry is not in a favourable position in so far as the number of young men engaging as apprentices and trainees is concerned, and

Inquiries of the Ministry to bring forward suggested plans for improvement. Those who participated expressed satisfaction with the manner in which the conference was conducted, and also expressed the opinion that the conference would be beneficial in all parts of Canada. About seventy-five delegates were in full-time attendance representing employers in the manufacturing and construction trades, organized labour, and provincial and federal officials responsible for the administration of apprenticeship and training legislation. All provincial governments were represented. So far as the specific recommendations of the conference are concerned, wide publicity has been given to them in the newspapers, and we would be willing to give a copy of the minutes of the conference to any hon. member who would be interested in reviewing them.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 246, to amend the Canada Grain Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when I spoke on the resolution I outlined very briefly the amendments which are being proposed. I also referred to the work and responsibilities of the board of grain commissioners and to the problem of overages at country elevators. Two or three of the amendments really require very little more explanation than I have already given.
It is proposed to increase the salaries of the chief commissioner and of his fellow commissioners. Their present salaries were fixed in 1930. In view of the magnitude and importance of the board's operations, there can be no question that the increases are well warranted. Certainly they cannot be considered excessive as compared with the rise of general salary levels either in the public service or in business circles.
The amendment to provide for the reappointment of members of the board simply removes any room for doubt concerning the authority to make reappointments. The present section was not considered sufficiently clear in this respect.
The position of assistant commissioner for the eastern division-the lakehead-is to be dropped. Experience has shown that the duties of that position can very well be undertaken by the board and staff at the headquarters in Winnipeg. I am satisfied that the board's operations at the lakehead will in no way suffer as a result of this change. The same amendment proposes that henceforth the salaries of the assistant commissioners shall be fixed by the governor in council.
Section 85 of the Canada Grain Act specifies the form in which tickets and other documents used by elevator operators must appear. Hon. members from the prairie provinces will be familiar, for example, with the book in which

cash tickets are kept. Some elevator companies now are considering adopting the modern system of a continuous form used in a registering machine which keeps locked-in carbon copies and which has a number of advantages over the current form of book. The present wording of section 85, however, prevents the use of such a machine. It is therefore proposed, by amending section 15, to give the board of grain commissioners authority to permit the use, in the alternative, of such forms as may be approved by the board. At least one operator of a country elevator system is experimenting with the possibility of combining into one operation the issuance of the cash ticket and the wheat board's producer's certificate. At the present time the elevator agent has to complete the cash ticket on one form and the producer's certificate on another. Using the new type of continuous form it is proposed that the original copy will be the cash ticket; copies 2 and 3 will be the producer's certificate and the remaining copies will be the required additional copies of the cash ticket. Thus, in one operation, both forms will have been completed. I have in my office a copy of the proposed set of forms which I shall be pleased to show to any hon. member who is interested.
The Canada Grain Act now provides that the board of grain commissioners may make regulations and orders in respect of a number of matters, but it does not empower the governor in council to make regulations. It is desirable that such authority should be vested in the governor in council in order to permit speedy action to be taken when the occasion demands it. It is proposed, therefore, to provide the governor in council with the powers specified. The explanatory notes to the bill draw attention to the fact that it is occasionally impractical, or even physically impossible, to comply with some specific requirement of the act. There is probably no other major line of business in this country in which more unforeseen contingencies of one kind or another can arise than in that of getting the grain crops forwarded from the harvest fields to commercial positions. Serious emergencies inevitably occur from time to time. For example, in the situation that existed last autumn the terminal space at the lakehead was so urgently needed that it was impractical to carry out the weigh-overs within the period required by the Canada Grain Act. Other emergencies are bound to occur in future but it is not possible to forecast what form they will take.
As regards the questions of regulations, the board's power is limited to regulations
Canada Grain Act
or orders that "are not inconsistent with this act". The governor in council is to be given power to meet exceptional circumstances by issuing regulations of a type that the board is not authorized to make.
Hon. members will note that it is proposed that any regulation made by the governor in council, dispensing with a requirement of the act, shall automatically expire on the last day of the next succeeding session of parliament. If, therefore, the difficulty that gave rise to the regulation were of a permanent nature there would be opportunity to introduce at that session an appropriate amendment to the act. In most cases, however, the problems are likely to be of a temporary nature and the regulation by the governor in council would meet the situation without the necessity of subsequent amendment to the act.
Finally there is an amendment to effect some slight but necessary changes in the definition of certain grades of grain. The only changes are to insert the minimum weights per bushel of the various grades mentioned.
I believe the provisions of the bill are entirely non-contentious. There will be differences of opinion about matters not dealt with in the bill. But since this is an overhaul of the Canada Grain Act, after the bill receives second reading it will be referred to the committee on agriculture for further examination. If the committee decides to add to or to amend the bill the government will be prepared to give due consideration to such recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly am pleased to hear the minister say that the bill will be referred to the committee on agriculture. As is realized, the duties and responsibilities of the board of grain commissioners are important and varied, as they have to do with the trade-in, storing, and transportation of grain in this country.
As I suggested before, I hope the minister will make it possible for the committee on agriculture to hear the views of the chief chemist who acts under the board in connection with the testing of grain, and has something to do with grading. It would be important to have this official appear before the committee, and also that we should hear officials from organized agricultural groups, such as the chief officials of the United Farmers of Canada, the Federation of Agriculture and others. They should be permitted to appear before the committee on agriculture and make recommendations and

Canada Grain Act
suggestions as to what should be done by way of amendment to the Canada Grain Act.
Their opinions vary. Some of them are not in agreement with the manner in which the act has been carried out, and I think it would be only right and proper that they should be given an opportunity to express their views. There has been considerable controversy in western Canada about the ultimate disposition of overages. The minister has said there would be no amendment in that respect. Nevertheless these people who have made a study of the matter should be permitted to make their recommendations. This bill is important to the grain producers in the prairie provinces. Because it is being referred to the committee on agriculture, I do not wish to speak at greater length now.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the minister is going to let this bill go to the committee on agriculture, because this will save prolonged discussion in the house, and give hon. members an opportunity to go into the Canada Grain Act. For some things there will be approval, and for others disapproval; but in committee we will have an opportunity to express our views and to ask questions. I do not think I need to say more at this time.

Mr. Speaker, like hon. members who have spoken thus far in the debate, those of us in the Social Credit party welcome the amendments to the Canada Grain Act. This act has been developed over a number of years, and the improvements it has brought about have been of great assistance to the farmers, particularly those in the prairie provinces. I am glad the minister has promised to send it to the committee. I hope he will have people there to give us information.
I am glad also that the minister has said that consideration will be given to an amendment that might be suggested by that committee. While the act is not nearly as bad as it used to be, I believe there is still room for improvement. Perhaps by the time the committee and the house are finished with it, it will be in a more satisfactory condition than it is at the present time.

speechtext:
More than two months ago, Mr. Speaker, I brought to the government's attention the very serious change that is taking place in the Toronto islands by virtue of erosion. I pointed out that if this damage was allowed to continue, the islands would disappear, and without their protection Toronto harbour would cease to exist. I urged the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) to send an engineer to see what could be done in the way of building a breakwater and groynes to prevent further deterioration.
On May 9, in order to check up on the progress that had been made in this matter, I put a question on the order paper as follows:
Has the government received a report from the engineer sent to investigate the damage caused by flooding and erosion to the Toronto islands?
If so, what is the recommendation of the engineer for protective works to prevent further deterioration?
The answer I received to both of those questions was as follows:
Matter under investigation.
Having received that return, Mr. Speaker, today I phoned the mayor's office in Toronto to see just what sort of co-operation the city of Toronto was receiving from the federal authorities. I was told that, first of all, the situation with regard to the deterioration of the Toronto islands had become considerably worse in the last two months. Secondly, the government has given no indication whatever that it intends to accept any responsibility in this matter. The reply that I received to my question is therefore simply a parliamentary way of saying that the government is doing nothing in this matter; intends to do nothing; and simply hopes that the matter will be forgotten.
I should like once again to point out to this government that the Toronto harbour is a vitally important part of the St. Lawrence seaway project, and that, without the Toronto islands, the Toronto harbour would cease to exist. The preservation of the Toronto harbour is a federal responsibility. If the Toronto islands are allowed to deteriorate further, many times the cost of protecting them now will have to be spent later in providing protective works to make the continuance of Toronto harbour possible. I take this opportunity, therefore, of once again strongly urging the government to recognize its responsibility, and to undertake, in co-operation with the city of Toronto, the protective works that are necessary to prevent further deterioration of the Toronto harbour.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, consideration has been given to that matter, but it has been found it is not a matter that can be dealt with separately. May I just ask one further question of the Prime Minister in connection with that matter? I appreciate the reason that universities were especially dealt with. I appreciate the difficulty of acting in advance of general principles being laid down. However, I ask the Prime Minister this question. Is it, as I understand it to be, a fact that the drama movement is perhaps, after a good many successful years, in danger not only of falling on evil days but perhaps of even coming to an end because of the failure of its resources? page 379, I notice that last year there was an item of $75,000 for publication of consolidation of statutory orders and regulations and there is no similar item this year. Was that something which was just for one year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for bringing this matter to my attention at this time because I felt that it was desirable that I have the opportunity of giving some information to the committee about it.
This item of $75,000 was recommended and voted the last time for the French version of the consolidation of the orders and regulations, and it was fully expected that it would be expended before March 31. As a matter of fact, only a small portion of it was expended because the printing office had more urgent work to be done and has not yet completed this French version. When the estimates were prepared it was anticipated that this $75,000 which was voted last year would be expended and that there would be no requirement for anything of that character this year. It so happens, however, that most of it has lapsed and in the supplementary estimates there will have to be an item for that portion of the $75,000 which was not expended and which will come to be paid during the present fiscal year.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Federal district commission-
318.	To provide for maintenance and improvement of grounds adjoining government buildings at Ottawa, and to authorize an amount not exceeding $142,400 for construction, improvements, maintenance and operation of the parkway system, under
£Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood).]
the control of the federal district commission which is additional to the sum of $300,000 granted by chapter 55, statutes of 1927, as amended, $433,794.

Yesterday in the public accounts committee we had some discussion about the amount voted for the federal district commission, and it was stated by the Auditor General that each year there is a deficit because the grant is not sufficiently large to pay their expenses.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Have the proceedings of that committee been reported to the house?

No, Mr. Chairman, they have not; but if I may say so, we are discussing this item at the present time and I am suggesting that if it is not large enough, it ought to be made larger.
I was going to point out that I think in the public accounts other revenue was shown from which they apply money to meet the deficit. I did not, however, rise especially to speak on that matter.
I understand that it is part of the duties of the federal district commission to look after the Mackenzie King bridge. I was wondering whether those who were responsible for advocating it could tell us whether the expenditure-which has been a large one-on that construction has been justified by the amount of traffic that is using it at the present time and whether there are any other plans for bringing a greater proportion of the traffic, especially at rush hours, across that bridge. From observations I have made from time to time, it seems to me that the bridge is not used a great deal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The approaches on this side of the Mackenzie King bridge have not been completed. It was hoped that the structures that stand in the way could be taken down early this spring, but the Minister of Public Works has not yet found a place to put those public servants who now have their offices in the buildings. That is the reason why the approaches have not been completed.
I have been over the bridge on several occasions and I agree with the hon. gentleman that if there was not going to be more traffic over it than there is at the present time it would not have been justified. But these approaches are going to be provided just as soon as other accommodation can be found for the offices that are now in the structures that have to be torn down. I hope that will not be long, because in the meantime the public is not getting annual value for the amount of capital that has gone into the construction of the bridge. That situation should therefore not be allowed to continue for any longer than is necessary.

Further on the same subject, may I say that I am delighted to hear from the Prime Minister that no one is going to be put out from shelter which he now has in order to accommodate the traffic which is going over that bridge. I think what he says is manifestly true, namely that up to the present time traffic has been extremely light.
May I ask the Prime Minister whether the operation and maintenance of Laurier house is under this item of the federal district commission or whether it is under public works?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will remember the terms of the legislation which was passed last year. As I recollect it-and of course I am speaking now only from memory-it was public works that was to maintain the structures and the federal district commission was to maintain the grounds at Laurier house; but the legislation requires the Minister of Public Works to maintain the structures that are there.
Any question as to the alterations of the building and the extent to which it is used as a centre of research would probably remain-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When Public Works
estimates are under consideration would be the time to ask about the alterations to the buildings.

Last year on this item I suggested two things: One, a revision of the federal district statute, which has been amended from time to time. Since that time I have consulted with the chairman of the federal district commission, and he has advised me it is the intention to look into the act and to make a report to the Prime Minister. The second thing I had in mind at the time was that since the work of the federal district commission and the national capital planning committee is very important and rather elaborate, and since the support of the house and of the public throughout Canada is very important toward the development of this district today, I think that not so much to investigate but rather to inform the members of this house it would be desirable that once in every parliament we should have an opportunity to bring the members of the federal district commission who are on the executive side before a committee to discuss their problems, and also their objectives. That was done a few years ago, I think, in two or three meetings before the banking and commerce committee in the other place. The suggestion is worth while, and if that were done hon. members and the public 55704-168J
Supply-Privy Council would realize the importance of the work much better than they do at the present time.
Some things have been said about the Mackenzie King bridge. I might be the lone rider on it from time to time, but I think in time the construction of the bridge will be justified. The approaches are not completed and the traffic has not been routed from other parts of the city. There is no doubt that it is a fine bridge and the people of Ottawa are very proud of it. I am quite sure that in time its construction will be justified.

I think the hon. gentleman will admit that the chairman of the federal commission is doing a great public service in the performance of his duties as such, just as his predecessors did, and the hon. gentleman is in frequent communication with the president. I can assure him that when he and the president come to me and tell me it would be of value to have a committee set up to enable hon. members to get information directly from the members of the commission, I shall be glad to give serious consideration to having that done as soon afterwards as possible.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Can the Prime Minister tell us the state of this fund? This is the fifth payment into it. It would add up to quite a sum of money. Can he tell us how much has been spent and what projects are under contemplation at an early date?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sorry but 1 have not got the actual expenditures out of the fund. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I shall be glad to do so, and have the federal district commission prepare a statement and the amounts. At the earliest possible occasion I will lay it on the table of the house.
Perhaps the Prime Minister will note particularly the developments around Sussex street with respect to the two bridges and also the razing of the old statistics building in the near future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have a note which has just been sent to me and which should have reached me earlier. It will enable me to dispose of the former question at once. It is from Mr. Cram and reads as follows:
It occurred to me that it might be well to insert in the estimates book of the Prime Minister an item of the expenditure made to date from the national capital fund.
Including the fiscal year 1951-52 four instalments of $2,500,000 each have been appropriated by parliament to the national capital fund.
Of this $10 million the following expenditure has
been made to date:
1.	Acquisition of property	 $1,158,600
2.	Mackenzie King bridge construction 1,264,700
3.	Construction of railway cut-off line
in south Ottawa	 413,700

Will the
Prime Minister remind me of what I should not have to ask? How long do these instalments go on-indefinitely? I refer to the annual contribution of $2,500,000.

It has to be renewed every year. The statement that was made when the first appropriation was recommended to parliament was that it might be advisable during each year for ten years to recommend to parliament the appropriation of an equal amount and this is the fifth time the government has brought the annual recommendation to parliament.
There is no commitment by parliament with respect to future appropriations, but the original general intention was, and it is still the intention, to recommend each year during the period of ten years this grant of $2,500,000.

These are substantial amounts that have been spent and I should like to know whether the expenditures are made by the relevant departments, the Department of Public Works for example, or is it done entirely by the planning commission itself?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand that for the construction of this bridge the federal district 'commission enlisted the services of the Department of Public Works and it was that department that finally certified the plans and specifications and tenders for the implementation of those plans were called for by that department.
I take it from that that the national planning commission does not maintain a separate staff and there is no duplication of any kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They do not maintain a capital construction staff; they maintain a maintenance staff to take care of the properties entrusted to them.

Can the
Prime Minister tell us whether the planning commission or the district commission intends to embark upon any major undertakings in the near future? It seems to me that this money is piling up. I understand the principal project they have in mind is the removal of the railroad tracks and the railroad station to some distance outside the centre of the city.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There has already been expended from the capital planning fund on that project a total of $413,700 for the railroad cut-off in south Ottawa. That is the first step in the carrying out of the project to remove heavy traffic trackage from the centre of the city. I think the intention is to co-

operate with the government and other public authorities in timing the public works that the commission will undertake. They do not want to place a heavier drain on materials and manpower than the Department of Public Works feels would be proper in connection with the things under its control, nor do they want to go beyond what we recommend to provincial governments and municipalities in the way of a co-operative effort to discourage inflation.

This question may not be altogether germane to this particular item, but it would seem to me that the federal district commission is not receiving sufficient money each year to carry out its current duties. Apparently it is spending more than $300,000 a year and I was wondering if consideration has been given to that fact.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Up to the present time the fund to which this $300,000 a year is contributed has not been exhausted; it is still in the black, to use a common expression. It is quite true that in the last couple of years more has been taken out than has gone in by way of annual appropriation and no doubt consideration will have to be given to keeping the account in a fluid condition. It has not yet been found by the commission or by the Auditor General that there is any urgency, but the matter is under consideration and the government will not hesitate to take the responsibility of recommending an increase when the commission and the Auditor General feel that an increase is required to keep the account in balance.

speechtext: 169. Office of the secretary to the governor general, including the salary of the secretary to the governor general at $7,600 additional to salary authorized by chap. 182, R.S. 1927, $120,224.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What progress is being made with a matter that comes under this item concerning which the Prime Minister and I have had discussions on previous occasions? speechtext: I inquired if it would not be possible to make the proper permanent amendments to deal with the governor general's establishment. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
no. To authorize and provide, subject to the approval of the governor in council, for expense allowances to the lieutenant governors of the provinces for travelling and hospitality undertaken in the exercise of their duties, ?86,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I do not intend to debate this item at length, but I do wish to repeat the opposition to it which we of this group expressed when the same proposal was first made earlier this session in the form of a supplementary estimate. That supplementary estimate provided for the institution of these special expense allowances to lieutenant governors for travelling and hospitality. The reason it was provided by way of a supplementary estimate was to permit the practice being made effective as from January 1 of this year.
We opposed that supplementary estimate and our further thought on this matter leads us to feel that we should still oppose a grant of this kind. We feel that if a case can be made for adjusting the salaries of the gentlemen who occupy these posts of lieutenant governor, then that adjustment should be made by statute in the salary itself.
We dislike the idea of the sliding scale that is involved in this matter. By the way, that reminds me that the Minister of Finance answered a question of mine when we were on the supplementary estimates as to why the wording was different in the supplementary estimates from the main estimates. He indicated that an amendment would be made at this time. I take it that amendment will be

Supply-Privy Council forthcoming and that it will set out the sliding scale formula. It seems to me that is unrealistic. I feel that to put these gentlemen in the position of having to turn in statements as to what they have spent on travelling and entertainment is hardly compatible with the nature of their positions. As I recall it, the Prime Minister said they were not going to be asked to submit definite vouchers covering every item of expense but rather that they would be asked to submit their own statements that they had spent whatever amounts were claimed. We feel it is wrong in principle to make a provision of this kind. We say again that if it is felt necessary to make any salary adjustments- not that we think any increase is necessary- it should be done by an adjustment in the salary itself rather than in this way. For these reasons we are opposed to item 170.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
To carry out the undertaking given by the Minister of Finance when the question arose on the supplementary estimates, I would ask my colleague, the Minister of Public Works, to move that the language of the vote, without affecting the amount, be changed to read as follows:
To authorize and provide for the reimbursement to the lieutenant governors of the provinces of Canada of the costs of travelling and hospitality-incurred in the exercise of their duties up to a maximum per annum for each as follows:
(a)	where the population of the province at the last decennial census did not exceed 500,000, $5,000;
(b)	where the population of the province at the last decennial census exceeded 500,000, $5,000 plus $1,000 per each 100,000 or fraction of 100,000 of population over 500,000, but not exceeding $12,000 in any case...

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I so move.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It sounds like a new formula for redistribution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is a new formula for the distribution of an amount not exceeding $86,000 to provide for the reimbursement of expenditures that the lieutenant governors feel they must incur to discharge properly the responsibilities of the offices to which they have been appointed.

I wish to say a word about this item. We have certain questionings about it. There are one or two questions I should like to ask. I take it that the expenses of the lieutenant governors last autumn when the royal party was here were in fact paid either by themselves or by the various provinces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

May I ask
whether this action is being taken on the initiative of the government itself simply as a thing which it seemed reasonable to do


or if in fact the matter was put forward by the provinces. It is hard for me to believe, for example, that the province of Ontario should not, could not and would not look after an expenditure of that kind. I wonder if we might be told a little more about the background, although the amount involved is quite trifling compared with some of the amounts we pass.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It has been brought
forward on the initiative of the government itself. Since I have been a member of the government considerable difficulty has been experienced on various occasions in securing gentlemen looked upon as of the right standing in their respective communities to assume the responsibilities of the office. It was pointed out to us by a number who have not become lieutenant governors that they could not afford to do it because they would have to spend very much more than what would be left of the salary fixed by statute after paying income tax. There was one suggestion that they should not be subject to income tax.
It was felt that as long as the requirements of the country were such that there had to be a very wide base for income tax, then exemptions from income tax were not the right thing to recommend. When you start making exemptions for one it leads to another. The officials of the Department of Finance and the minister felt it would be creating embarrassment for future ministers of finance to commence the process of exempting individuals from income tax. However, it is recognized that there are certain expenses that are necessarily incurred to receive the income, and recognition that certain expenses are incurred as a condition of getting the income that is taxed is being extended almost from session to session. The only way in which it was felt it could be done in this case was to recognize that there were such expenditures.
I have no doubt that the lieutenant governor of Ontario is going to expend considerably more than this amount but it was felt that here was something that was comparable to allowances made to ministers or ambassadors abroad, and that an amount of this kind would make it somewhat easier to secure the acceptance of gentlemen who might be approached in the future with the offer to occupy this very dignified and honourable office. I was told in one case, and it was not in Ontario or Quebec, that it meant an annual expenditure of not less than $40,000 out of the personal income of the incumbent to discharge properly the responsibilities of the office of lieutenant governor in the manner to which the people of his

Supply-Royal Canadian Mounted Police
province had become accustomed. I felt they had perhaps become accustomed to more than was really necessary but that nevertheless there was a certain amount that was inevitably required to do the things that we frequently ask lieutenant governors to do.
We frequently communicate with them and ask them to take some part in the entertainment of distinguished guests who are visiting our country. Constitutionally the responsibility for the appointment and emoluments of lieutenant governors is a responsibility of the central government. It was felt that if there was a certain amount against which they could say they had made the kind of expenditures that are described in this language as proper expenditures in the discharge of the functions of their office in a dignified way it would be proper to reimburse them not in the form of income but for necessary expenses that they had incurred.

speechtext: 422. General administration, $367,953.

Mr. Chairman, unless the
minister wishes to make an opening statement, I shall proceed to ask some questions, the first of which concerns the manner of payment of the salaries of members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I think perhaps it would be better to have this discussion under the general item.
It was represented to me that many members of the force, if not all, receive their salaries monthly rather than bi-monthly, and that this imposed upon them considerable financial difficulty in that they do not have enough at one time to meet household expenses as they become due. On the other hand, if they have household expenses at the end of the month, then before receiving the monthly cheque at the end of the following month they experience some financial embarrassment.
I understand representations have been made asking that they be placed on a basis whereby they would be paid twice a month, but that so far nothing has come of it. Is the minister able to say whether this matter is receiving attention? I hope he will tell us that it will be changed so that members of the force may receive their cheques twice monthly.

speakeroldname: Hon. Sluari S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is a fact, as my hon. friend
has said, that the members of the force are paid once each month. I must say however that I have received no representations from anyone to the effect that this method has not been acceptable to members of the force. I have asked the commissioner, who is now sitting in front of me, and he says he has received no representations. So, as the hon. member's remarks are the first representations made to us, we shall be glad to look into the matter, to see if they have some foundation.

I am glad the minister has said that, because I was under the impression that representations had been made in writing. My information was on the basis of personal conversation, so I am not in a position to offer substantiation. If the minister will look into the matter, I shall be grateful.
What provision is the minister making to see to it that the incomes of mounted police are kept in line with the increased cost of living? Have adjustments been made in their incomes?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Provision was made in December of last year whereby an increase was granted to the salaries of members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police at about the same time and, so far as the two bodies are comparable, on the same basis as was awarded to members of the civil service.
Is there a general feeling among the mounted police that they are being adequately paid to meet the expenses they have to incur?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Subject to the feeling all of us have, that we would like to have our incomes somewhat larger than they are, I think there is a general feeling in the force that they have been treated fairly, in comparison with, let us say, the civil service or other bodies with whom they would be comparable. I am sure they would agree, however-as indeed I would myself-that their incomes could be larger than they are. I might say the same about mine, too.

Let us suppose a member of the force is transferred from one place to another, and upon doing so finds it impossible to obtain living quarters at the rate he had been paying before the transfer. Is there any follow-up item by officials to see that such a situation does not become serious?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
While I cannot say that all such cases are taken care of, for some years past it has been our practice to increase the number of buildings, residences and the like available for members of the force in the different cities in which detachments are placed. We add to that number as finances
2670	HOUSE OF
Supply-Royal Canadian Mounted Police and materials permit. In respect of some officers we rent premises, and make them available.

What provision is made to cover additional expenses incidental to the arrival of another member of the family? This is a serious matter for married people. Is there any provision for additional expense incurred upon the birth of a child?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I wonder if I may be permitted to restate my hon. friend's question so that I shall be sure to have it right. Does he refer to the mere addition to the family of a member of the force, or is he referring to the additional cost of moving from one detachment to another arising through the having of a larger family?
I understand we do not defray the cost in connection with an addition to the family of a member of the force. But, inasmuch as we pay the moving expenses in. the event of a man's being moved from one detachment to another, naturally these would include the expenses of all members of his family. And of course if he has had an addition to his family, we would pay the moving expenses if any of that additional member.

The impression is abroad everywhere that we pay our mounted police meagrely, and that they are kept pretty well on a subsistence basis. If additional expense is incurred through an incident such as that I have indicated, or through sickness in a family which would cause a burden of debt to be developed, is some provision made for cushioning any such conditions which may develop, and which would affect the head of the household?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In common with all other Canadians, members of the force receive family allowances. When there is an addition to the family there is automatically qualification for a greater family allowance, for that addition. Their moving expenses are paid when they transfer from one detachment to another-and that is more than some Canadians receive when they are moved from one place of business to another. Then, during the last two years the members of the force have received two separate and fairly substantial increases in their pay. In each case the effort was made to keep the members of the force on a basis comparable with members of the civil service, and in a manner which would be fair to the civil service on one hand and the members of the force on the other. When all these factors are taken into consideration I think we can claim that the members of the force have been fairly treated in respect of the matters to which the hon. member has referred.
In the details at page 472 the revenue is set out. Is that revenue received from the provinces by way of payment for work done by the mounted police in those provinces?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member is referring to the $2,658,155 on that page?
That is the amount for 1950-51.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is made up almost entirely of payments received from provincial and municipal governments in eight of the provinces for police services supplied by the R.C.M.P. under contracts with those provinces and municipalities.
Does that money go into the consolidated revenue fund?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
423. Operation and maintenance, $25,210,272.

Under this item, Mr. Chairman, there is a considerable increase in the number of personnel on the administrative side-I do not mean the members of the force itself- from 588 to 790. Would the minister say what has been the main cause of that increase?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The reply is that the major portion of the increase is accounted for by the naturally heavy increase in security work which is being done by the mounted police consequent upon the condition of cold war in which we are at the present time. This security work, as I am sure the hon. member will realize when he reflects upon it, involves a lot of desk and paper work. In addition to that, we have tried to get civilian employees into all positions in the force in which they could discharge the duties of the office, in order to release as many of the force as possible for active police work.

There is no similar figure given for the actual number of men, non-commissioned officers and officers in the force itself. There is an item here for the pay of the members of the force, but can the minister say what is the present total of the personnel of the force as compared with last year?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I have the figures here. As at May 24, 1952 the force in regular uniform totalled 4,213; special constables, 371; civilian employees, 340; civil servants, 780; total, 5,704.
I think the minister said 340 civil servants are included? What are those w*ho are represented by this 340? Are they doing police work or office work or administrative work?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are doing not only office but maintenance work as well, not police work.
Are they the ones the minister referred to as special constables-I believe that phrase was used.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The special constables do special police work of various kinds.
Are they in uniform?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, they are not. Just to avoid any misunderstanding on that score, what is referred to as the special branch of the force, which is engaged in security work, would take in uniformed men, special constables, civilian employees and civil servants, so it cuts right across those four categories. As I have said, the special constables do special police work of various kinds.

I might say that from what small experience I have had with them I have been favourably impressed. It has always seemed to me they were considerate. At the same time I should like to know, because it is of such great importance, what the minister can say to us regarding the selection and training of these men. After all, if I understand their duty correctly, they have that extremely difficult task of considering andi making up their minds as to the loyalty of Canadian citizens, and they have the responsibility of actually reporting against people.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think perhaps I can indicate the degree of care which is exercised in the selection of members of the special force, if I indicate that in the choice of the members of the regular force we ordinarily accept about one-twelfth of those who offer themselves as recruits. You are
speaking now of the uniformed men, the 4,000?

I wonder if the minister can say a word with reference to the security work done by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the work carried on by the civil service itself. I have been quite concerned about this when hearing recently of the security check which is made of civilian employees, for instance, in the Department of National Defence. Then we find the Department of Defence Production has certain security forms which must be filled in before people are employed. speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am afraid my knowledge of the details of the administration of these other departments to which the hon. member refers is not sufficient for me to state at all authoritatively what their security precautions are. Nevertheless I think I can explain quite accurately the relationship between these other departments and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
The other departments of government, depending on how vulnerable they may consider themselves to be in the matter of security, ask the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for a report upon any employee concerning whose loyalty they entertain doubt. This report is prepared by men in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who are specially detailed for that purpose. After that report has been prepared it is sent to the deputy minister of the department concerned. I should like to emphasize the point that in no case does it contain any recommendation by the mounted police to the effect that the subject of the report should be either dismissed or retained. The report is entirely factual. When it is received by the deputy minister

As far as the mounted police are concerned, their duty is confined in this context to the supplying of factual reports concerning employees of other departments.

Can the minister say whether the screening-to use the general word which is used-which is done in other departments is always done by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police at their request, or whether these other departments also carry on their own screening? June 2 or 3 in 1953. But I do

Will the minister say

My hon. friend's second observation, that it is partly for accounting purposes that they are set up in this way, is correct.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Well, as I am sure my hon. friend will appreciate, it is impossible to have an air service, however small, without having some administrative officers that look after the air service as such. But the headquarters staff, including not only the highest officers, but most of the high officers are over and command all these *services. These increases in pay, coupled with a pretty active recruiting campaign, have resulted, for example, in an increase in the uniformed force from 3,650 in 1951 to 4,213 in 1952. To what extent do the provincial governments rely upon the mounted police to do their policing? What supplementary provincial forces are there in the provinces? Can the minister tell us that?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. I might reply to my hon. friend's questions in these terms. In eight of the provinces of Canada, that is, in all the provinces except Ontario and Quebec, the entire provincial responsibility for policing is carried out under contract by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. In every one of those eight provinces there is just one police force, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, which does all the federal work, for the federal government directly, and which under contract does all the law enforcement and administration of justice which is the constitutional responsibility of the provincial authorities.

In addition to that we do the work for a number of municipalities in the different provinces. In Prince Edward Island, 1; Nova Scotia 3; in New Brunswick, 8; in Manitoba, 18; in Saskatchewan, 27; in Alberta, 21; in British Columbia, 45, or a total of 123 municipalities, involving 451 members of the force, also under contract, for which substantial payments are made. These are the moneys the hon. member for St. John's West referred to as having come into the consolidated revenue fund from the provinces and the municipalities.
Does the municipality itself enter into a contract, or does it do that through the province?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Each contract is with each municipality separately. It is in most cases between the municipality represented as a rule by the mayor and secretary-treasurer, the province represented by the attorney general of the province, and myself representing the federal government. Each municipality has a contract which it renews periodically under which we look after the policing of that municipality.

Was it necessary to employ more personnel owing to the fact that we have been confronted with an increased amount of smuggling in the last year or two? Was it necessary to employ any more personnel, or was it taken care of by the staff already appointed?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, it was not necessary to increase the personnel for the purpose to which the hon. gentleman has referred. What we did was to concentrate our anti-smuggling personnel in the force at various vulnerable points along the border at which there seemed to be a concentration of smuggling. In that way we were able to handle it without incurring any additional expense for personnel.
What is the basis of co-operation between Ontario and the federal government in respect to policing? Does Ontario have some assistance from Ottawa?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I am quite correct in saying that the most harmonious relationships exist between the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the provincial forces of both Ontario and Quebec. They are mutually helpful at all times, but Ontario has its own police force and looks after all its own policing responsibility itself. So has Quebec. Other than this mutual help there is no connection between the two forces.

Just to follow up the question asked by the hon. member immediately to my left about the smuggling, we have seen statements in the press from time to time that the volume is so extensive with respect to
[Mr. Garson.1

cigarettes that presumably-I think I have seen this statement-only a relatively small percentage can possibly be caught. Is that correct or does the department or the force feel that it has the necessary personnel and resources to deal with and trace down at least the large proportion of the present volume of cigarette smuggling?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a rather embarrassing question in the sense that it is hard for any force, no matter how competent it is, to make a positive statement that it has apprehended all smugglers, or a certain percentage of them. I think on the whole, measured in terms of seizures, prosecutions and the like, the force not only feels it has been quite successful in its anti-smuggling operations but has substantial grounds for so feeling.

Is the minister going so far as to say he feels that the resources of the force are sufficient to enable them to deal with, perhaps I should say, well over half the actual volume of smuggling, or does he and the force feel that to deal with that percentage they would have to have considerably more resources?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the answer to my hon. friend's question is to be found in the statement I made a few moments ago, that we were able to deal with this smuggling with our existing personnel by concentrating at the points at which most of the smuggling was taking place. I am quite sure that if the high officers of the force had felt they needed more personnel for that purpose they would not have hesitated to detail them. If I may draw a parallel, when dealing with a heavy increase in its work the special branch did not hesitate at all to add substantially to its membership. Where the work was to be done they did not hesitate to increase their personnel. In dealing with this smuggling the force felt that their trained men properly distributed among the most vulnerable places could cope with the situation as well as any force could cope with it. There never was a police force in history that eliminated all crime. The most that any force can do is deal with an optimum percentage of crime. I think the percentage in this case has been gratifying to the force and that they have substantial grounds for their gratification.

In order that we may have a background for this discussion, has the minister available, first, the number of cases in which smugglers were apprehended during the fiscal year 1951-52 as compared with 1950-51 and, second, the total number of

cigarettes which were seized in the last fiscal year as compared with the preceding fiscal year?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The commissioner tells me that the crime statistics for the past fiscal year are just being completed. For obvious reasons we have not made a practice of publishing the statistics or boasting about our accomplishments but I would be glad to see that this comparison is made available to my hon. friend as soon as we get the figures.
Who would be responsible for dealing with smuggling over the boundary between Ontario and the United States? Would that responsibility rest upon the mounted police or the Ontario police?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As my hon. friend, knows, the Customs Act was passed by this parliament and therefore the prevention of smuggling is the responsibility of the federal police force. In provinces like Ontario and Quebec where they have provincial forces and a federal police force as well, the prevention of smuggling falls squarely upon the federal police force.

branches of police work which are specifically a federal responsibility?

narcotics.

The minister said they were able to deal with this smuggling with the existing personnel. I do not want to fall into the error of accepting every rumour as though it was an authenticated fact, but there is a widespread belief, which I have never heard seriously questioned, that the smuggling of cigarettes was not on a retail basis, that it was on a completely wholesale plan. If I may
interrupt, I think in a way that is a fair inference, but the minister does not need to infer because I asked a definite question whether in fact the force was satisfied and whether they had asked for any further assistance.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I was just coming to that. As I say, I would respect perhaps even more the views of professional men in police administration. I said before, and I repeat, no requests were made by the force for additional personnel for anti-smuggling work because it was thought, as I am informed, that the existing staff of highly trained men, if concentrated at the points at which most of the smuggling was taking place, would achieve what I might call an optimum law enforcement. It is impossible to get 100 per cent anti-smuggling enforcement. As a matter of fact no person knows what percentage the force does get because you do not know how many get through. Men who have been professionally engaged in this type of work for a long period of years can form what at best is only a professional opinion that they can get the optimum result by a certain method. In the present case it was their

Supply-Royal Canadian Mounted Police view they could get that optimum result by concentrating their existing personnel, who would be trained and able people, and not by taking on people who were green at that particular type of work. That is what they did.
Maybe, as my hon. friend rather hints, that was a wrong decision. I myself would think it was a sound decision, and I would not be deterred from that view by any of the newspaper items upon this subject. We have placed in the hands of the two hon. members on the official opposition side of the house who have taken part in this debate the figures as to what was done in the way of seizures and so on. These figures show an over-all increase of 42-9 per cent. That is a very large percentage increase to take place in one year.

These very figures seem to me to raise a serious question. If I understand the figures correctly, they show that the increase in cases in 1952 over 1951 with respect to federal statutes-and the minister said that was chiefly smuggling- was 42 per cent.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

He said that the increase in Criminal Code cases was 37 per cent, and in provincial and municipal cases 46 per cent. If I read the figures aright, instead of finding there is a tremendous preponderance in the cases connected with smuggling, actually the increase there is not as big as in provincial and municipal cases. That would seem to me to cast doubt. I take it nobody doubts that there was any amount of material to work on there, yet the percentage is not as high.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I submit with great respect that the conclusions which my hon. friend is trying to draw from these figures are invalid.
Just a simple seeker after truth.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I am myself; but I do not think by that conclusion my hon. friend is catching up with it. I suggest that when you consider the great variety of traffic offences, government liquor control offences and all the other provincial and municipal offences, you cannot draw a comparison between those and these federal offences. The significant thing, however, is that the real comparison here is between federal offences which took place in 1951 and federal offences which took place in 1952. The federal offences with which the mounted police have to do are limited in number. They are mainly in the field of customs work and narcotics. Where you have


an increase in one year of 42-8 per cent, approaching 50 per cent, in federal offences, I would say it indicates a very high degree of stepping up of activity.

I would be impressed if it were not for these other figures and the fact that it is not going to be as high as in these other cases where there is no special reason to believe there was an additional amount of crime.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I suggest, as I have already suggested, that no conclusions can validly be drawn from a comparison of the increase in provincial and municipal offences on the one hand and the increase in federal offences on the other hand. Taking a rather absurd example, let us suppose that some of the municipalities for which we are acting take it into their heads to overhaul their traffic bylaws and are determined to prevent jaywalking and all kinds of traffic or parking offences. This could produce a great bulge in your statistics of municipal offences which would have no significance whatever for the purpose for which my hon. friend is trying to use it. Perhaps it would have been more judicious on my part if I had not stated the Criminal Code offences and the provincial and municipal offences at all, and had simply directed my hon. friend's attention to the increase in federal offences, because that is really what we are talking about.

I appreciate the fact that the minister gave me the facts, although I would expect the Minister of Justice to always do that. However, I still find one argument he has made very unconvincing. He says there are all kinds of crimes that arise under municipal statutes, and no doubt there are; but he has not suggested, and I doubt if he can suggest, that there was any special event which happened which would tend to increase greatly the amount of crime in that category. At any rate, there was nothing comparable to what everyone I have talked to believes has been going on along the frontier in the matter of the smuggling of tobacco. Surely the minister will not tell me that was not an outstanding case of evasion of law; yet we have only a 42 per cent increase. I am sorry that the Minister of Public Works feels so badly.
