speechtext: That is not fair.

He said he was anxious to spend it and I am giving him credit for it. But we want to know what expectation the minister has of getting the work done. We are all agreed it should be done. Last year for reasons which we have not yet been told, but which no doubt are valid, the amount was not spent. What we are asking is whether the Minister of Justice or his colleague the Minister of Public Works, who seems so restless at the moment, can give us some idea as to what work is going to be done. We do not want money spent just for the sake of spending it; we want money spent for the sake of getting results. I am sorry three of us have had to make this point; but it is important.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think the conclusions my hon. friend draws from figures are always valid. I think the last conclusions he has drawn are invalid.
I did not draw any conclusions.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What is my hon. friend's reasoning? He looks at page 474 of the estimates and sees that out of an authorized expenditure of something more than $4 million last year there was an actual expenditure of a lesser amount.
Just half.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He immediately jumps to the conclusion that the amount we wish to have authorized this year is not going to be spent.
I just asked a question; I did not jump to any conclusion.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think there is any reason, in logic, for that conclusion. I have already said everything it is possible for me to say, and that is that this estimate has been brought down seriously, that the facilities are needed. We are not anxious to spend money for the sake of spending money in the way the hon. member for Greenwood has indicated, but we are anxious to have badly needed buildings, and the fact that the provision of those buildings involves legitimate expenditures of money is incidental. But when the hon. member says he wants me to give the House of Commons an assurance that the money is surely going to be spent, then I say he is asking me to launch out into the realm of prophecy. The spending of it will depend upon actions of people who are outside the control of our department-contractors who


do the work, for example. It will depend upon whether they can get on with their work and complete it in time.
As to the suggestion that any other minister will stand in the way, I say there is no foundation for that at all. These estimates are brought down by the government. They are the government's estimates. They are serious estimates, and we are asking this committee to vote the money. We do not ask hon. members to vote estimates we do not intend to spend. But if, for example, some of the buildings are in northern locations where the frost comes early, and where there might be a freeze-up a month earlier than is normal, do hon. members expect the minister to underwrite that sort of thing by way of a prophecy, just in order to satisfy members of the opposition?
The minister has said I am jumping to conclusions. I have not jumped to any conclusion. I asked him a simple and pertinent question.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member was asking me to jump to conclusions, and I did not wish to do so.

The minister has indicated that he was either unable or unwilling to spend more than half the amount which was actually appropriated in the estimates last year. Now, I said, what reason has the minister to suppose-this was my question and if he will think for a minute he will remember this was the way it was put-that this year he will be in a position to spend the total amount asked, because the amount asked this year is even more than he asked last year. That was the question I was seeking to have answered, and I do not think we have had it answered yet because the minister has not been able to give us any facts upon which an opinion can be based. Has the material situation improved, or have the contractors assured him they will be able to do the work this year? I shall ask the minister why it was not possible to spend this amount last year, and whether the situation which caused last year's position has changed?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Having regard to the fact that it is not our department that spends this money, I could not oblige the hon. member with the reasons. May I say with great respect that I wonder if we are not labouring a rather obvious point. I have had to do with the preparation of government estimates for some fifteen years now; and with our climate in this country I do not know of any government which authorizes public works items like these that is able in every year to spend all that has been voted by parliament. They all try, as we are doing here, to appropriate

what they want to spend. If there is a shortfall, there is a shortfall. It is rather routine business in most governments.
In some cases the grant lapses, and it is just voted again another year, but in other cases it may not lapse. There is no human being who can prophesy, at the time we are voting these estimates, for example, the weather conditions under which they may have to be spent. No person knowing the way in which these estimates are brought up ever says that we should attempt to prophesy-
Yes, they do.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, they do not.

We are being asked here to vote a matter of $4 million. The minister who is the head of this department is no different from the head of a department in a private corporation, outside of the fact that he is spending the taxpayers' money. Apparently suggestions come to the ministers of this government, and when their estimates are being considered they walk in and ask for an amount of money. They try to put it through in spite of the endeavour of the opposition to find out what this money is for, and why the taxpayer is being called upon to cough up this amount of money to carry out the desire of somebody, not the minister. The minister is only the railroader of the grant.
Can you imagine the Steel Company of Canada making an addition to their plant at Hamilton, Ontario, and having the man in charge of production come before the board of directors requesting $2 million or $5 million and not being able to explain the purpose for which that money was to be used? We have just had an example of a minister talking about a total amount of $4 million and not being able to explain why $2 million, or about 50 per cent, was not spent. He says it was on account of climatic conditions. We have not heard from the minister that he has investigated this situation to such an extent that he could say that 50 per cent of the $4 million is going to be spent in Alaska or that it is not going to be spent in Alaska. He does not know where it is going to be spent. He has tried to indicate to us, the watchdogs of public funds, that climatic conditions or frost conditions prevented the expenditure. You would think that this country was snowbound from the United States border up to the north pole.
We are looking for an explanation as to why the money which was requested last year was not spent. We have not heard from the minister that it was because the Eskimos could not lay bricks. We have heard that you cannot tell about weather conditions. Just imagine such nonsense. Weather conditions
Supply-Royal Canadian Mounted Police may make it impossible to spend 50 per cent of the money being collected from the taxpayers. If the minister knew anything about why he was asking for this money, we would be fair and decent about the situation. If he could say that 50 per cent of the money about which I am asking is going to be spent in a part of Canada where climatic conditions may not permit $1 being spent, we would say, "Certainly you cannot prophesy about conditions there." We know as well or even better than he does that certain contractors will not even tender in the tough sections of the country.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman-

I let you speak without interruption, and now you let me speak. You may ask me all the questions you like when I have finished, and I shall give you intelligent answers. Here is a man asking us to pass an item which is only $4 million, but which may form part of the $700 million surplus which this government is requesting. I am sure every hon. member in this house must be dumbfounded to find a minister requesting this amount of money who knows so little about the reasons for the request. The only argument advanced in favour of giving him this money carte blanche is that weather conditions may prevent the spending of it. He does not say it is for this or for that.
As I said before, we do not wish to handicap this important department in any way; give them all they need without any restraint whatever, but when the minister asks us to pass an item and only mentions weather conditions during the four times he has been on his feet, then it is time to ask for further explanations. I know that I live in a cold but pleasant country. From the way the minister speaks, you would believe we are snowbound twelve months a year from the United States border to the northern part of the Northwest Territories. My colleagues want to know if the minister has the slightest idea why this money is necessary, and why the money that was voted last year was not utilized. The only argument he has given us so far-I would defy him to refute my statement-is that you cannot tell about weather conditions. Never in my life have I heard such weak nonsense from any minister who was trying to obtain money from the already overburdened taxpayers.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after this
impassioned oration-
It may be, but I hope it sank in.

Don't take it too seriously.
2680	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Royal Canadian Mounted Police
That is the trouble, you don't.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member says he wants the details of these expenditures. It did not require a twenty-minute speech for him to get the details.
It did, from three different members.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall now give him the details which I forbore giving before because I did not think it was necessary to take up the time of the house to go into details of this sort. I hope he will listen carefully; and if he knows anything about Canadian geography, he will know that weather conditions at some of these places might have a great deal to do with whether this work could be completed before the construction season runs out.
I have been in every part of Canada, just as you have.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I admit that, and that is why the hon. member will understand this reference when I give it. I shall give the places where this construction will take place. The first is Fredericton, New Brunswick; there is no weather problem there.
That is not snowbound, either.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No
one is trying to stop you from talking.
If you will listen for a minute you might learn something.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
We
know how much you know.
Outside of Quebec, you don't know anything.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that interjections be reserved until we get this list on the record. The places are, Fredericton, New Brunswick; Long Island, Ontario; Rockcliffe, Ontario; Toronto, Ontario; Moose Factory, Ontario; Port Harrison, Quebec;-my hon. friend knows where that is; that is quite far north-Norway House, Manitoba; Regina, Saskatchewan; Stony Rapids, Saskatchewan; Cumberland House, Saskatchewan; Beaverlodge, Alberta; Vancouver, British Columbia; Eskimo Point, Northwest Territories. Perhaps the weather would have some effect there.
It would.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Fort McPherson, Northwest Territories. Would it have some effect up there? I think it would. Liard, Northwest Territories; Cambridge, Northwest Territories; Hay River, Northwest Territories; Ak-

lavik, Northwest Territories. Perhaps the weather would have something to do with it up there.
It would.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Simpson, Northwest Territories; Arctic Red River, Northwest Territories; Whitehorse, Yukon Territory. Newfoundland: construction of detachment quarters all along the rock-bound coast around the whole of Newfoundland where the material has to be brought in by boat and where difficulties not so much of weather but in the matter of communications are encountered. That is the list of the locations. If my hon. friend's knowledge of Canadian geography is as great as he claims it to be-and I believe it is- I think he will agree that when you are talking about Aklavik and all these places I have mentioned here, in which the mounted police function as well as in the cities of Canada, the time of the fall freeze-up and the like would have a great deal indeed to do with whether you could get your money expended within the fiscal year.

Mr. Chairman, after going over the geography of Canada, may I ask how much of the amount of $4 million being asked is being expended in places that are affected by climatic conditions? Come on; give us the amount.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
On these Newfoundland
detachment headquarters all around the entire coast of Newfoundland, reached only by boat, on that one item alone there is over $1 million.
Out of the $4 million?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; out of the $4 million.
Is that part of the country weather-bound any time during the 365 days of the year?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I suggest that my hon. friend ask his fellow member behind him not as to whether it is weather-bound by cold but as to whether there are not at these places problems of communication, freight shipment and the like, and of getting materials in to do the work.

Can the
minister say where these headquarters are being constructed?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At places all around the coast of Newfoundland. I could give my hon. friend the details.
Will the minister give the names of the places?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Harbour Grace, Hawkes Bay, Ferryland, Glovertown, Harbour Breton,

Hampden, Burgeo, Baie Verte, Twillingate, Deer Lake, Stephenville Crossing, Claren-ville, Stephenville, Whitbourne, Burin, St. Lawrence and Placentia.
Only two or three of those would be ice-bound during the winter and spring.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not suggesting that it is merely a question of being ice-bound. I am suggesting that by reason either of cold weather, as in Aklavik for example, or by reason of difficulties of communication, or of their being storm-bound at certain periods, or because of other difficulties which have to do with the ease of construction, when these buildings are to go up in an isolated locality it makes a great deal of difference as to whether we can get men in within a certain period of time, as compared with say Rockcliffe or Toronto.
When my hon. friend stops to reflect he will realize that when we are talking about the Royal Canadian Mounted Police detachment buildings being constructed at these isolated points, we are undertaking an entirely different type of construction problem from that which we would have in a large city. There is the problem not only of weather, but of getting skilled tradesmen out to an isolated area, away from the city where they are now in great demand. Having regard to all the problems which arise in connection with the construction of these buildings, I do not think that my hon. friends of the official opposition, who like to be fair-as a rule they are very fair-would want to question our statement that there is a difficult problem in getting this work completed at these places, and berate me because I cannot get up and honestly say to my fellow members: "I am sure that if you vote $4 million, it is all going to be spent come next January". I cannot do that. No honest man could.

I should like to say only this. I do not think the minister is quite right in saying there are special difficulties in most of these places. Most of the places he has mentioned are well known and are accessible at almost any time of the year.
Places in Newfoundland, you mean?
It is places in Newfoundland that I am speaking about. I should say there is no special difficulty with regard to most of those places.

Supply-Royal Canadian Mounted Police Pensions and other benefits-
430.	Pensions to families of members of the mounted police who have lost their lives while on duty, as detailed in the estimates, $6,863.

I should like to ask the minister whether, when they took over the Newfoundland Rangers, the men received the pension rights under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and whether their families can also benefit from the pension fund created for the families of the mounted police.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. When the Rangers were taken into the Royal Canadian Mounted Police their pension rights were protected, subject to their paying for their service in the other force; that is, in the Rangers force. That was done on the same basis as that upon which-

Was the
basis the same as that on which the civil service of Newfoundland was taken in?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot say whether it was the same as the civil service, but I know that it was the same basis as that upon which we took over the British Columbia provincial police. In taking over those provincial police forces we have to preserve, as regards pension rights, a parity between the various provincial forces. That is where the comparison is made. We applied to Newfoundland the same principle that we had previously applied to British Columbia.
Under this item 430, at page 476 of the details I notice that the amounts are quite different. I should like to ask what is the principle on which the amounts are fixed?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The pensions are paid to families of members of the mounted police who have lost their lives while on duty, and the amount which is paid is half the pay to which the deceased mounted policeman was entitled.

Have the increases been occasioned by the fact that he would now have been in receipt of more pay had he lived? Is that the occasion for the increase? I am not complaining about the increases, because they are all small. We should just like to know the basis of it; that is all. I suppose it is because salaries have increased in the meantime.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. These are, in substantial part, old cases which have been carried on under this allowance when it was created. There was not always a provision in the statute for a pension of that sort, and prior to that provision being made there was a separate item in the estimates to take care

Supply-Justice
of it. These are a carryover, and the adjustment is as between their previous status and the new status under this new statute.

Does the minister intend to make any general statement on introducing the estimates of his department? I would suggest that if he sees his way clear to do it, he might do so by a particular reference to two subjects: First, the way in which he proposes to deal with amendments to the Criminal Code; and second, the report of the royal commission on combines legislation. I make that suggestion for this reason. If we are to be told, as perhaps we are, that it is still intended to introduce the bill on the Criminal Code during this session, then it would suggest, at any rate, that we do not now pursue too closely any inquiries into the Criminal Code and that whole subject. In the same way if the minister can tell us what the proposal is with respect to the report of the committee on combines legislation, if we did ask questions at least they would be more pertinent to that question than if we just covered the whole field. Therefore I think it would be appreciated if the minister would make some sort of statement on at least these two subjects.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know whether it has come to the attention of the hon. member, but a bill on the Criminal Code was introduced in the Senate and is being considered there now by a Senate committee. It will come back to this house in due course and be debated on second reading, and again in committee. Therefore I would be merely anticipating the debate which would have to take place in any case. Indeed I doubt very much whether I would be in order, debating at another time in the house a matter which is already under consideration, having regard especially to the fact that it was mentioned in the speech from the throne and therefore cannot be anticipated in a debate of this kind.
I was really seeking information as to whether it is to be proceeded with at this session.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, yes.
There have been rumours to the contrary.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They are unfounded. Certainly so far as the Department of Justice and the government are concerned the intention is to proceed with the new Criminal Code at this session. It has been introduced in the

Senate; it will be dealt with there, and it will come back here and be passed. A great deal of work has been done on it already. The work of the committee which prepared it extended over a period of three years. They did a really good job, and consequently we should not have much trouble with it.
With regard to the report of the Mac-Quarrie committee, that has been received and tabled. Only today the Prime Minister and I signed the resolution which is to go on the order paper leading up to the Combines Investigation Act amendment bill. This as a money bill. It will be introduced in the course of the next day or so, and will go through the ordinary routine.
I did not think there was any other part of the Department of Justice that required any introductory remarks by myself, with the possible exception of the penitentiaries. When we get to that item I might make a short statement reviewing the major developments of the last year, which might not be too apparent from a hasty reading of the annual report.

175. Administration of justice-miscellaneous expenditure, including expenses of litigated matters, $21,200.

There is a matter on which I want the minister to comment. I am sure he will have read, and with a great deal of interest, the report of an address by General J. A. Clark, Q.C., of Vancouver, the president of the Canadian Bar Association, to the Alberta section of the bar association. The article dealing with appointments to the bench was reprinted starting on page 28 of the January issue of the Canadian Bar Review. General Clark makes a number of most interesting comments. It is late in the day to start a general debate on the matter if, indeed, such should be necessary. But the starting point of my approach to this would be the reference he makes to the resolution passed by the bar association in 1949, as follows:
That the government of Canada be requested to consult with a committee consisting of the chief justice of the province and the chief justice of the trial division and representatives of the benchers of the law society in the province mentioned before making any appointment to the bench of that province.
As a starter I was going to ask the minister to make some reference to that resolution, and indeed to the whole matter of the article, because it is an important one. It is four minutes to six, and I do not know whether the minister feels that he could cover it in four minutes. I rather doubt it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not really think one could cover it in four minutes. As my hon. friend indicates, this is a very important matter, one which is worthy of comment and upon which I would be most happy to make some comments, because while I agree with many of General Clark's observations I do not by any means agree with all of them, and I would very much like the opportunity to indicate the ones with which I do not agree.
Could we call it six o'clock?

o'clock. Perhaps when we meet again the minister will be able to let us know what the conditions of employment, salaries and pensions are vis-a-vis one another.
